items.prose: A cereal maker fills boxes labelled 750 g. Its filling machine has a known sd of 18 g a box. A trading-standards officer suspects underfilling and weighs 36 boxes: their mean is 743.1 g. Her plan fixed the level $\alpha = 0.01$ before she weighed anything.

parts.question: Which pair of hypotheses fits the officer's test?

options.why: 743.1 g is the sample's mean. The null names the value the boxes should have, the label's 750 g.
A null must fix one value of $\mu$, so that surprise can be measured. The officer's suspicion goes in $H_1$.
The officer suspects underfilling only. That names a direction, so the alternative is one-sided.

feedback.correct: The null is the label's mean, 750 g, and the suspicion of underfilling is the one-sided alternative $\mu < 750$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the label's value in $H_0$ and the officer's suspicion in $H_1$.

byKey.sample-null: 743.1 g is the sample's mean. The null names the value the boxes should have, the label's 750 g.
byKey.swapped: A null must fix one value of $\mu$, so that surprise can be measured. The officer's suspicion goes in $H_1$.
byKey.two-sided: The officer suspects underfilling only. That names a direction, so the alternative is one-sided.

explain.text: A null fixes one value, here the label's 750 g. Underfilling is a direction, so $H_1: \mu < 750$.

parts.question: What is the standard error of the mean of the 36 boxes, in grams?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The mean of $n$ boxes has standard error $\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$.

byKey.over-n: You divided by 36. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{36} = 6$.
byKey.variance: That is $\tfrac{18^2}{36}$, the variance of the mean. The standard error is its square root.

explain.text: Averaging 36 boxes shrinks the spread by $\sqrt{36} = 6$, so the mean's standard error is $\tfrac{18}{6} = 3$ g.

parts.question: Using the standard error of 3 g from part 2, what is the $z$ statistic? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the null mean from the sample mean, then divide by the standard error.

byKey.sign: You took 750 minus 743.1. The statistic is the sample mean minus the null mean, so it is negative here.
byKey.over-sd: You divided by the sd of one box, 18 g. The mean of 36 boxes has standard error 3 g.
byKey.carried: You used a standard error of 0.5 g, from dividing by 36. With 3 g, $z = -2.3$.

explain.text: The mean sits 6.9 g below the label, and one standard error is 3 g. So $z = -2.3$: the mean is 2.3 standard errors below 750.

parts.question: Using $z = -2.3$ from part 3 and the alternative from part 1, what is the p-value? You are told $\Phi(2.3) = 0.9893$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. With $H_1: \mu < 750$, the p-value is the area below the observed $z$.

byKey.upper-tail: That is $P(Z \le 2.3)$, which a reversed subtraction in part 3 also gives. With $H_1: \mu < 750$ the p-value is the lower tail, $\Phi(-2.3) = 1 - 0.9893$.
byKey.two-sided: You doubled the tail. The officer's alternative is one-sided, so only the lower tail counts.

explain.text: The curve is symmetric, so the tail below $-2.3$ equals the tail above 2.3: $1 - 0.9893 = 0.0107$. Luck alone gives a mean this low about one time in 93.

parts.question: Using $p = 0.0107$ from part 4, what should the officer conclude at her planned level $\alpha = 0.01$?

options.text: Fail to reject $H_0$: 0.0107 is above 0.01, though the boxes may still be underfilled

options.why: The plan fixed $\alpha = 0.01$ before the weighing. Moving to 0.05 after seeing p breaks the plan.

options.text: Accept $H_0$: the boxes hold 750 g on average
options.why: Failing to reject is not proof. A test cannot show that $H_0$ is true.

options.text: Reject $H_0$: there is only a 1.07% chance that the boxes are filled correctly
options.why: A p-value assumes $H_0$ is true. It is not the chance that $H_0$ is true, and here it does not pass the level.

feedback.correct: $0.0107 > 0.01$, so the planned test does not reject. The mean is low, but not low enough for her strict level.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare p with the level fixed before the data, 0.01.

byKey.switch-level: The plan fixed $\alpha = 0.01$ before the weighing. Moving to 0.05 after seeing p breaks the plan.
byKey.accept: Failing to reject is not proof. A test cannot show that $H_0$ is true.
byKey.chance-null: A p-value assumes $H_0$ is true. It is not the chance that $H_0$ is true, and here it does not pass the level.

explain.text: The rule is to reject when $p \le \alpha$. Here 0.0107 is just above 0.01, so she fails to reject. That does not show the boxes are full.

items.prose: A phone maker advertises 19.5 hours of video on one charge. A reviewer plays video on 8 phones until each runs flat. The hours are 15, 19, 20, 17, 18, 16, 21 and 18. She suspects the true mean is below the advert. Treat the 8 lives as independent draws from a normal distribution.

parts.question: What is the sample mean $\bar x$, in hours?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the 8 lives and divide by 8.

byKey.n-minus-one: You divided the total, 144, by 7. The mean divides by the count, 8.

parts.question: Using $\bar x = 18$ from part 1, what is the sample sd $s$, dividing by $n - 1$?

feedback.correct: The deviations from 18 are $-3, 1, 2, -1, 0, -2, 3$ and 0. Their squares sum to 28, so $s^2 = \tfrac{28}{7} = 4$ and $s = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each deviation from 18, add them, divide by 7, then take the square root.

byKey.divide-by-n: You divided 28 by 8. The sample sd divides by $n - 1 = 7$, because $\bar x$ was estimated from the same data.
byKey.variance: That is $s^2$. The sd is its square root.
byKey.carried: You measured the deviations from 20.571, the mean found by dividing by 7. From $\bar x = 18$ the squares sum to 28, so $s = 2$.

explain.text: Dividing by $n - 1 = 7$ allows for measuring spread about $\bar x$, which was fitted to the same data. So $s = \sqrt{\tfrac{28}{7}} = 2$ hours.

parts.question: Using $\bar x = 18$ and $s = 2$, what is the $t$ statistic for $H_0: \mu = 19.5$? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The standard error is $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt 8} \approx 0.7071$ hours, so $t = \tfrac{18 - 19.5}{0.7071} \approx -2.121$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide $\bar x - 19.5$ by $\tfrac{s}{\sqrt n}$.

byKey.root-seven: You divided $s$ by $\sqrt 7$. The curve has 7 degrees of freedom, but the standard error uses $\sqrt n = \sqrt 8$.
byKey.over-s: You divided by $s$ itself. The mean of 8 phones has standard error $\tfrac{s}{\sqrt 8}$.
byKey.sign: You took 19.5 minus 18. The statistic is the sample mean minus the null value, so it is negative here.
byKey.carried: You used $s = 1.871$, from dividing by 8. With $s = 2$ the statistic is $-2.121$.

explain.text: $t = \tfrac{-1.5}{2/\sqrt 8} = -0.75\sqrt 8 \approx -2.121$. It follows the $t$ distribution with $8 - 1 = 7$ degrees of freedom.

parts.question: Using $t = -2.121$ from part 3, which conclusion is right at 5%? One-sided 5% cut-offs are 1.645 for the normal and 1.895 for $t_7$. The two-sided 5% cut-off for $t_7$ is 2.365.

options.text: Reject $H_0$: $-2.121$ is below $-1.895$, the one-sided cut-off of $t_7$

options.why: She suspects a mean below the advert, which names a direction, so the test is one-sided. 2.365 splits the 5% over two tails.

options.text: Reject $H_0$, because $-2.121$ is below $-1.645$, the normal cut-off
options.why: The decision is right but the reason is not. With $\sigma$ estimated from 8 phones, $t$ follows $t_7$, whose cut-off is 1.895.

options.text: Reject $H_0$: the phones' true mean is 18 hours
options.why: Rejecting says that 19.5 hours is hard to square with the data. It does not pin the true mean at the sample's 18.

feedback.correct: With 7 degrees of freedom the one-sided cut-off is 1.895, and $-2.121 < -1.895$. The 8 phones reject the advert at 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the side from her suspicion, and the curve from how the sd was found.

byKey.two-sided: She suspects a mean below the advert, which names a direction, so the test is one-sided. 2.365 splits the 5% over two tails.
byKey.normal: The decision is right but the reason is not. With $\sigma$ estimated from 8 phones, $t$ follows $t_7$, whose cut-off is 1.895.
byKey.pins-mean: Rejecting says that 19.5 hours is hard to square with the data. It does not pin the true mean at the sample's 18.

explain.text: Her suspicion names a direction, so the test is one-sided, and an sd estimated from 8 phones gives $t_7$. Its lower 5% cut-off is $-1.895$, and $-2.121$ lies beyond it.

parts.question: Other adverts could be tested with the same 8 phones. Use the standard error 0.7071 hours from part 3 and the cut-off 1.895 from part 4. What is the smallest advertised mean they reject at 5%? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the advertised mean that puts $t$ exactly at $-1.895$.

byKey.normal: You used the normal cut-off 1.645. With $s$ estimated from 8 phones, the cut-off is 1.895.
byKey.two-sided: You used 2.365, the two-sided cut-off. Her test is one-sided, so it uses 1.895.
byKey.wrong-side: You subtracted. An advert is rejected when it sits far above the sample mean of 18, so add $1.895 \times 0.7071$.
byKey.sd-not-se: You multiplied the cut-off by $s = 2$. The test measures the gap in standard errors, 0.7071 hours.

explain.text: Any advert of 19.34 hours or more is rejected at 5%, and any below it is not. The real advert of 19.5 hours sits 0.16 hours inside that range.

items.prose: A wine taster says she can pick the dearer of two wines blind. In each of 12 trials she tastes a pair in random order and names the dearer one. If she is only guessing, each trial is right with chance $\tfrac12$, independently, so the $2^{12} = 4096$ right-wrong sequences are equally likely. Her claim is tested one-sided at 5%, and $W$ counts the trials she gets right.

parts.question: Under $H_0$, what is $P(W \ge 11)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: There are $\binom{12}{11} = 12$ sequences with 11 right and 1 with 12 right, so $P(W \ge 11) = \tfrac{13}{4096} \approx 0.0032$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the sequences with 11 right and with 12 right, then divide by 4096.

byKey.eleven-only: You counted 11 right only. 12 of 12 is at least as extreme, so add its one sequence.
byKey.twelve-only: That is 12 of 12 alone. Add the $\binom{12}{11} = 12$ sequences with 11 right.

explain.text: Choosing the single trial she misses gives 12 sequences, and one sequence has every trial right. So 13 of the 4096 sequences have 11 or more right, and $\tfrac{13}{4096} \approx 0.0032$.

parts.question: Using the 13 sequences from part 1, what is $P(W \ge 10)$? There are $\binom{12}{10} = 66$ sequences with exactly 10 right. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the 66 sequences with exactly 10 right to the 13 from part 1.

byKey.exactly-ten: That is $P(W = 10)$ alone. At least 10 right also takes the 13 sequences with 11 or 12 right.
byKey.carried: You added 66 to 12, leaving out 12 of 12. With it there are 13 sequences above 10, so 79 in all.

explain.text: With the 13 from part 1 there are 79 sequences with 10 or more right. So if she gets 10 right, the p-value is $\tfrac{79}{4096} \approx 0.0193$.

parts.question: Using $P(W \ge 10) = 0.0193$ from part 2, what is $P(W \ge 9)$? There are $\binom{12}{9} = 220$ sequences with exactly 9 right. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the chance of exactly 9 right to part 2's answer.

byKey.exactly-nine: That is $P(W = 9)$ alone. Add $P(W \ge 10) = 0.0193$ from part 2.
byKey.carried: You added $P(W = 10) = 0.0161$ only. With 11 and 12 right included, $P(W \ge 10) = 0.0193$, which gives 0.0730.

explain.text: $\tfrac{299}{4096} \approx 0.0730$. If she gets 9 right, guessing alone matches or beats that about 7 times in 100.

parts.question: Using parts 2 and 3, what is the smallest number right that rejects $H_0$ at 5%?

feedback.correct: $P(W \ge 10) = 0.0193 \le 0.05$ but $P(W \ge 9) = 0.0730 > 0.05$. So 10 right rejects and 9 does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the smallest count $k$ whose p-value, $P(W \ge k)$, is at most 0.05.

byKey.nine: 9 right has p-value $P(W \ge 9) = 0.0730$, above 0.05. The tail starts at the count observed, so use $\ge$, not $>$.
byKey.eleven: 10 right already has p-value 0.0193, which is at most 0.05. So 10 rejects; 11 is needed only for a 1% test.

explain.text: The p-value of $k$ right is $P(W \ge k)$. It first falls to 0.05 or below at $k = 10$. So she needs at least 10 of 12 to convince a 5% test.

items.prose: A pizza chain promises a mean delivery time of 30 minutes. A food blogger times 16 of its deliveries, and their mean is 33.5 minutes. She tests $H_0: \mu = 30$ against $H_1: \mu > 30$ at 5%.

parts.question: Head office says delivery times have an sd of 8 minutes. Taking that as the known $\sigma$, what is $z$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide $\bar x - 30$ by $\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$.

byKey.over-sd: You divided by $\sigma = 8$. The mean of 16 deliveries has standard error $\tfrac{8}{\sqrt{16}} = 2$ minutes.
byKey.over-n: You divided $\sigma$ by 16. The standard error divides by $\sqrt{16} = 4$.
byKey.no-null: You divided the whole mean by the standard error. Subtract the promised 30 minutes first.

explain.text: The mean of 16 deliveries has standard error $\tfrac{8}{4} = 2$ minutes. The blogger's mean is 3.5 minutes late, which is 1.75 standard errors.

parts.question: Using $z = 1.75$ from part 1, what is the p-value? You are told $\Phi(1.75) = 0.9599$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. With $H_1: \mu > 30$, take the area above the observed $z$.

byKey.two-sided: You doubled the tail. Her alternative is $\mu > 30$, so only the upper tail counts.
byKey.lower-tail: That is the area below 1.75. With $H_1: \mu > 30$ the p-value is the area above it.

explain.text: The upper tail beyond 1.75 holds $1 - 0.9599 = 0.0401$. On the $z$ test, the blogger would reject at 5%.

parts.question: She learns that the 8 minutes comes from the chain's quieter branches. Her own 16 times have sample sd $s = 9.6$ minutes. Using $z = 1.75$ from part 1, what is $t$ with her $s$ in place of $\sigma$? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Only the sd changes, so rescale $z$ by $\tfrac{\sigma}{s}$.

byKey.flipped: You scaled by $\tfrac{9.6}{8}$. A larger sd makes a larger standard error, so $t = 1.75 \times \tfrac{8}{9.6}$ is smaller than $z$.
byKey.over-s: You divided 3.5 by $s$ itself. The standard error is $\tfrac{9.6}{\sqrt{16}} = 2.4$ minutes.

explain.text: The standard error is now $\tfrac{9.6}{4} = 2.4$ minutes, so $t = \tfrac{3.5}{2.4} \approx 1.458$. It is judged on $t_{15}$, since 16 times give 15 degrees of freedom.

parts.question: Using $p = 0.0401$ from part 2 and $t = 1.458$ from part 3, what should she report? The one-sided 5% cut-off of $t_{15}$ is 1.753.

options.text: Fail to reject $H_0$: with her own $s$, $t = 1.458$ is below 1.753

options.why: That p-value rests on $\sigma = 8$, which describes other branches. With the sd estimated from her data, the $t$ test applies.

options.text: Fail to reject $H_0$, because 1.458 is below 1.96
options.why: The decision is right but the cut-off is not. Her test is one-sided with the sd estimated from 16 times, so it uses 1.753.

options.text: Accept $H_0$: deliveries take 30 minutes on average
options.why: Failing to reject is not proof. A mean of 33.5 minutes still hints at slower deliveries.

feedback.correct: With the sd estimated from her 16 times, $t = 1.458$ is judged on $t_{15}$. It is below 1.753, so she fails to reject; the $z$ test's 0.0401 used an sd that does not apply.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Decide which sd describes these deliveries, then use that test's cut-off.

byKey.z-rejects: That p-value rests on $\sigma = 8$, which describes other branches. With the sd estimated from her data, the $t$ test applies.
byKey.normal-cut: The decision is right but the cut-off is not. Her test is one-sided with the sd estimated from 16 times, so it uses 1.753.
byKey.accept: Failing to reject is not proof. A mean of 33.5 minutes still hints at slower deliveries.

explain.text: The $z$ test is right only when $\sigma$ is truly known. Her times are more spread out, so $t$ is smaller than $z$ and its cut-off is larger. The evidence is suggestive, but not enough at 5%.
